Label: balinese
Short Description: Split gate (candi bentar) marking the entrance to a Balinese Hindu compound or temple; the two symmetrical halves symbolise the duality of the universe.
Physical Specifications: Height: 3–8 m | Width: 2–5 m | Base footprint: 1–3 m deep | Material: red brick, paras stone, volcanic stone | Capacity: gateway only (no interior)
Forbidden Materials \/ Sacred Taboos: Iron nails forbidden   only stone, brick, and lime mortar. Sacred paras stone from specific quarries must not be substituted. No painting over ritual carvings.
Materials & Construction Techniques: Paras stone (soft volcanic tuff), red brick (bata merah), white lime mortar, carved volcanic andesite, black river stone base; dry-stack and lime-mortar joinery; hand-carved pepalihan (layered moulding)
Building Process & Rituals:
1. Choose auspicious date (dewasa ayu) with a pemangku (priest).
2. Ground-breaking ceremony (ngeruak tanah) with offerings.
3. Foundation stones blessed with holy water (tirta).
4. Walls built by undagi (Balinese master builders) using traditional proportions (asta kosala kosali).
5. Completion ceremony: melaspas ritual to spiritually activate the gate.
Philosophy & History (Fun Fact): The split design represents Mount Meru split in two   the cosmic mountain of Hindu cosmology. Candi bentar appear only in Bali; mainland Hindu temples use closed gates. The gap between the two halves is intentional: spirits and gods may pass freely, but evil is confused by the opening.
Etiquette & Rules for Entering \/ Living: Walk through the centre   never touch the gate walls unnecessarily. Women in menstruation must not enter a temple compound. Sarong and sash (selendang) required. Bow slightly when passing. Never turn your back to the inner shrine after passing through.

Label: Banten
Short Description: Stilt house of the Baduy Dalam and Baduy Luar communities; entirely hand-built from natural forest materials with zero modern tools or nails.
Physical Specifications: Floor area: ~6×4 m | Height off ground: 0.5–1 m | Roof pitch: steep 60° | Capacity: 1 nuclear family (~5 persons) | Orientation: always north–south
Forbidden Materials \/ Sacred Taboos: No nails, screws, cement, or any metal fasteners. No modern tools (saws, drills). No paint or chemical treatment. Electricity and pipes strictly forbidden inside Baduy Dalam territory.
Materials & Construction Techniques: Bambu tali (black bamboo) for walls and floor; eurih grass (Imperata) for thatched roof; wooden pegs and rattan lashing only; raised on wooden or bamboo stilts; no adhesives
Building Process & Rituals:
1. Elder (puun) selects the site and sets the north–south axis.
2. Forest materials gathered communally (no chainsaw   hand-cut only).
3. Posts set by hand; floor and walls woven/lashed with rattan.
4. Roof thatched by the whole community (gotong royong).
5. No formal ritual   construction itself is the ceremony; silence and focus are required.
Philosophy & History (Fun Fact): Baduy Dalam forbids photography, writing, and sketching of their homes. The house design has not changed in centuries by direct law of pikukuh (Baduy customary law). The steep roof sheds rain instantly   no gutters needed. Houses are rebuilt every few years as materials degrade; impermanence is part of the philosophy.
Etiquette & Rules for Entering \/ Living: Remove footwear before the ladder. Speak softly   loud voices disturb the house spirit. Guests sleep near the door, never in the inner room (imah). Do not ask to photograph the interior. Accept any offered food; refusal is impolite. No outsiders may enter Baduy Dalam without a guide.

Label: batak
Short Description: Grand communal longhouse of the Batak Toba; a single massive boat-shaped roof shelters an extended clan (marga), with no interior walls dividing family units.
Physical Specifications: Length: 15–20 m | Width: 8–10 m | Ridge height: 8–12 m | Capacity: 5–10 families (up to 80 persons) | Orientation: east–west (sunrise–sunset axis)
Forbidden Materials \/ Sacred Taboos: No iron nails   wooden pegs (pasak) and rattan only. The gorga (carved ornamental panels) may not be painted in non-traditional colours. The central post (tiang raja) must not be cut from just any tree   only specific species ritually selected.
Materials & Construction Techniques: Hardwood timber (ingul/teak) for main frame; bamboo for walls; ijuk (black sugar-palm fibre) for roof thatch; wooden pegs; rattan lashing; gorga panels carved from soft wood and painted in black, white, and red (singa motif)
Building Process & Rituals:
1. Clan head selects auspicious date with a datu (ritual specialist).
2. Mangase tano ritual: offerings buried at the four corner posts.
3. Main posts raised communally; tiang raja (king post) raised last with chanting.
4. Roof structure assembled on the ground then hoisted.
5. Completion: manomu ceremony   feasting, music, and blessing of the house spirit (begu).
Philosophy & History (Fun Fact): The dramatic upcurved roof ends (like a boat's prow) represent the Batak cosmological boat that carries souls between worlds. Gorga carvings are not decorative   each motif (singa, desa na ualu) is a spiritual protective code. A Rumah Bolon without gorga is considered spiritually naked.
Etiquette & Rules for Entering \/ Living: Enter by the single front door   never the back. Bow under the low entrance beam (a deliberate design to force humility). Elders and guests sit on the right side; women and children on the left. Do not step over anyone seated. Pointing feet toward the hearth is disrespectful. Clapping to call someone inside is rude   call by name.

Label: dayak
Short Description: Massive elevated longhouse housing an entire Dayak village under one roof; one of the longest traditional houses in the world, stretching up to 150 m.
Physical Specifications: Length: 30–150 m | Width: 10–15 m | Height off ground: 3–5 m | Capacity: 20–100 families | Orientation: parallel to the nearest river
Forbidden Materials \/ Sacred Taboos: No nails or metal fasteners in traditional builds. The central hearth area (awah) must not be built over. Sacred trees (kayu belian/ironwood) may only be felled after ritual permission from forest spirits (sangiang).
Materials & Construction Techniques: Belian (Borneo ironwood) for main posts and floor   naturally termite- and rot-resistant for 100+ years; bamboo and lighter timber for walls; sago palm or ironwood shingle roof; rattan lashing; hand-carved decorative panels (kalung)
Building Process & Rituals:
1. Shaman (balian) identifies the site through dream-divination.
2. Forest spirits (sangiang) petitioned with offerings before any tree is felled.
3. Main belian posts sunk deep   no concrete; friction and mass hold them.
4. Longhouse built section by section; each family unit added as the community grows.
5. Housewarming: gawai ceremony with music (sape), tuak rice wine, and three days of communal feasting.
Philosophy & History (Fun Fact): Rumah Betang is both house and village   the entire social, spiritual, and judicial life of the community happens under one roof. The longhouse chief (pambakal) holds court in the common veranda (sami). Ironwood posts from a 200-year-old betang are still standing today   ironwood is effectively indestructible.
Etiquette & Rules for Entering \/ Living: Always announce yourself at the base of the ladder before climbing. The common veranda (sami) is public; family rooms (bilik) are private   knock before entering. Remove shoes at the ladder. Guests are given a place on the sami, never the bilik. Do not walk between a person and the fire. Refusing tuak rice wine at a gawai ceremony is a serious social offence.

Label: javanese
Short Description: Refined aristocratic Javanese house centred on the iconic four-pillar pendopo (open pavilion); a refined spatial philosophy made architecture.
Physical Specifications: Pendopo: 10×10 m typical | Pringgitan: 4×10 m | Dalem: 8×10 m | Ridge height: 8–14 m | Capacity: extended noble family + staff
Forbidden Materials \/ Sacred Taboos: The four soko guru (central pillars) may never be replaced or moved   doing so is believed to bring misfortune to the family. The paringgitan threshold must not be blocked. Gebyok (carved partition walls) must not be painted over with non-traditional motifs.
Materials & Construction Techniques: Teak (jati) for all structural timber   prized for strength and grain; hand-carved gebyok panels; clay roof tiles (genteng); lime-plastered brick for lower walls; natural earth pigments for decorative painting; no metal fasteners in traditional construction
Building Process & Rituals:
1. Primbon (Javanese astrological calendar) consulted for auspicious dates.
2. Ground-breaking: slametan ceremony with yellow rice (nasi kuning) and prayers.
3. Soko guru pillars erected first   the most ritually significant act.
4. Roof structure (atap) assembled by undagi (master carpenters).
5. Moving-in ceremony: brokohan   offerings, prayers, and community feast.
Philosophy & History (Fun Fact): Joglo spatial zones reflect Javanese social cosmology: the pendopo (public) = outer world; pringgitan = transitional space (where wayang shadow plays are performed); dalem = private inner world. The taller the roof, the higher the owner's social rank   roof height was once regulated by the Mataram court.
Etiquette & Rules for Entering \/ Living: Guests receive only in the pendopo   entering the dalem uninvited is a grave breach. Remove shoes before the pendopo. Sit cross-legged or with legs folded sideways   never stretch legs toward elders. Speak in the appropriate Javanese register (krama inggil with elders). Never raise your voice inside. Walking with a slightly bowed posture shows respect.

Label: Maluku
Short Description: Open-sided sacred meeting house of Maluku; the spiritual and political heart of a negeri (village), where adat law is declared and ancestors are honoured.
Physical Specifications: Floor area: 8×12 m typical | Height: 4–6 m | Open on all four sides (no walls) | Raised on stone or wooden posts 0.5–1 m | Capacity: entire village assembly
Forbidden Materials \/ Sacred Taboos: No permanent walls may be added   the open sides are spiritually mandatory. Sacred stones (batu pamali) under the floor must never be moved or excavated. Certain wood species reserved for the main posts by adat law.
Materials & Construction Techniques: Sago palm timber for posts and beams; sago leaf thatch (rumbia) for roof; open bamboo or timber floor; stone foundation piers; no walls by design; traditional lashing with forest rattan
Building Process & Rituals:
1. Raja (village chief) and saniri (council of elders) determine the site   always at the village centre.
2. Sacred stones (batu pamali) placed at foundation before posts are set.
3. Community builds together; no outsiders may assist with the core structure.
4. Post-raising: suling (flute) music played continuously to call ancestor spirits.
5. Inauguration: cakalele war dance performed to activate spiritual protection.
Philosophy & History (Fun Fact): The baileo has no walls by design   ancestors must be able to move freely in and out. Every decision made inside a baileo is considered witnessed by the ancestors and therefore binding forever. The building faces the sea, as Malukan ancestry is maritime. Baileo cannot be sold, relocated, or structurally altered   it belongs to the negeri's collective soul.
Etiquette & Rules for Entering \/ Living: Men and women enter from different sides. No shoes inside. Sit according to your clan's designated position   seats are not interchangeable. Women may not enter during certain sacred ceremonies. Never speak above the voice of the saniri council. All decisions made inside must be honoured   leaving mid-assembly is deeply disrespectful.

Label: minangkabau
Short Description: Iconic matrilineal clan house with dramatic upswept roof horns (gonjong); owned and inherited exclusively by women across generations.
Physical Specifications: Length: 15–25 m | Width: 8–12 m | Gonjong horn height: 5–8 m above ridge | Rooms: 3–11 (odd number only) | Capacity: one matrilineal clan (suku)
Forbidden Materials \/ Sacred Taboos: The number of gonjong (roof horns) must always be even. Rooms must number odd. The rumah gadang may not be sold   only the matrilineal line may inherit. No structural changes without adat council approval. The front ladder faces away from the road (intentional).
Materials & Construction Techniques: Ijuk (black sugar-palm fibre) for dramatic gonjong roof; hardwood timber (surian/mahogany) for frame; woven bamboo (sasak) or timber for walls; hand-carved and painted panels (ukiran) in red, black, and yellow (Minang colours); no nails in traditional builds
Building Process & Rituals:
1. Penghulu (clan chief) sets auspicious date with the ninik mamak (elders).
2. Mancasuak tiang: first post ceremony   offerings, prayers, and the eldest woman of the clan strikes the first post.
3. Frame raised by communal labour (gotong royong).
4. Roof thatched last   the gonjong tips are the final, most celebrated act.
5. Batagak penghulu: house inauguration combined with the installation of the clan chief.
Philosophy & History (Fun Fact): The gonjong roof horns are said to represent the horns of a buffalo (kerbau)   referencing the legendary Minangkabau founding story where a small local buffalo defeated a larger Javanese one (the origin of the name Minangkabau = 'victorious buffalo'). The house belongs to the women; men traditionally sleep in the surau (prayer house) until married.
Etiquette & Rules for Entering \/ Living: Only women and children live in the rumah gadang permanently; husbands are guests in their wife's home. Guests enter via the front ladder. Remove shoes at the entrance. Sit on the floor   no chairs in traditional settings. Men visiting their wives announce themselves at the base of the ladder and wait. Never enter a closed room without permission.

Label: Nusa Tenggara (sasak)
Short Description: Traditional Sasak thatched-roof house and rice granary (lumbung) complex; the lumbung's distinctive top-heavy mushroom silhouette is Lombok's most iconic image.
Physical Specifications: Bale tani floor: ~5×4 m | Lumbung height: 3–5 m | Lumbung base: ~2×2 m (deliberately small to deter rats) | Capacity: 1 family + grain storage | Raised on short wooden posts
Forbidden Materials \/ Sacred Taboos: The lumbung roof must not be tiled   only alang-alang (cogon grass) thatch. The floor of the bale tani must remain earthen   no concrete or tile. Sacred rice (padi benih) stored in the lumbung may not be consumed   it is seed for the next season.
Materials & Construction Techniques: Alang-alang (cogon grass) for thick thatched roof   up to 1 m thick for insulation; bamboo frame and walls; earthen floor; wooden posts; rattan and bamboo lashing; no nails; the lumbung base is deliberately narrow to prevent rat access
Building Process & Rituals:
1. Kiai (Islamic scholar/elder) or adat elder selects the date.
2. Ground is cleared and levelled by the family.
3. Posts set first; roof frame constructed on the ground then raised.
4. Thatch layered from bottom to top   a family effort over several days.
5. Blessings read (doa selamat) upon completion; neighbours invited for communal meal.
Philosophy & History (Fun Fact): The lumbung (rice granary) is never just storage   it represents the family's prosperity and food security. The top-heavy silhouette (narrow base, wide overhanging roof) is functional: the overhang keeps rain off the walls and the narrow post-base stops rats from climbing. Today the lumbung shape is used for hotels and restaurants across Lombok as a cultural icon.
Etiquette & Rules for Entering \/ Living: Guests enter the bale tani from the front only. Remove shoes at the door. Sit on the tikar (woven mat) on the earthen floor. The inner room (bale dalam) is for the family   guests stay in the front room (bale luar). Never touch the lumbung without permission   it holds the family's rice reserves and is considered under the protection of Dewi Sri (rice goddess).

Label: Papua
Short Description: Circular thatched igloo-like dwelling of the Dani and Lani peoples of the Papua highlands; engineered to retain heat at 1,600 m+ altitude with no fireplace chimney.
Physical Specifications: Diameter: 4–6 m | Height: 2.5–3 m | Interior headroom: ~1.5 m (low by design) | Capacity: 5–10 men (honai) or women/children (ebei) | No windows
Forbidden Materials \/ Sacred Taboos: Men's honai and women's ebei must be completely separate structures. No outsider may sleep in a men's honai without elder permission. The central fire pit may not be extinguished during cold season   it is kept alive continuously.
Materials & Construction Techniques: Yar (wicker/woven reed) for cylindrical walls   tightly woven for insulation; runu grass (Imperata) for thick conical roof thatch; wooden posts and horizontal ring beams; earthen floor; no metal; central stone fire pit (no chimney   smoke seeps through thatch, killing insects and preserving the roof)
Building Process & Rituals:
1. Clan elder designates the site within the village compound (silimo).
2. Men of the clan fell and carry all materials from the forest.
3. Circular wall woven around a central post; ring beams lashed horizontally.
4. Conical roof frame assembled then thatched densely from base to apex.
5. No formal ceremony   first fire lit inside is the activation; the honai is 'alive' when the fire burns.
Philosophy & History (Fun Fact): The honai has no chimney by design   smoke from the central fire slowly permeates the thatch, hardening and waterproofing it while killing insects. This makes the roof last 15–20 years. The low entry forces everyone to bow when entering   a daily physical reminder of humility. Honai are gender-segregated: men sleep in honai, women and children in ebei, pigs in wamai.
Etiquette & Rules for Entering \/ Living: Announce yourself loudly before entering   never walk in silently. Bow to pass through the low entry hole. Sit close to the fire   warmth is communal property. Do not bring food from outside into the men's honai without offering it to all present. Women do not enter the men's honai. Elders sit furthest from the door (position of honour). Silence at night is required   the fire must not be disturbed.

Label: Toraja
Short Description: Ancestral clan house of the Toraja with a towering boat-shaped roof; the most spiritually powerful building in Toraja culture, tied to the identity of the living and the dead.
Physical Specifications: Length: 10–15 m | Width: 4–6 m | Roof overhang: up to 3 m front and rear | Ridge height: 6–10 m | Capacity: clan ceremonies (not permanent residence for most)
Forbidden Materials \/ Sacred Taboos: The tongkonan may not be sold, demolished, or relocated   ever. The main posts (a'riri posi') may not be replaced without a full ceremonial sacrifice. The carved and painted panels (pa'süra') must use only traditional colours: red, black, white, yellow. No modern paint permitted.
Materials & Construction Techniques: Bamboo for the layered, curved roof structure   dozens of layers create the dramatic upward curve; hardwood timber for frame; hand-split bamboo cladding for walls; carved and painted wooden panels (pa'süra') with Toraja motifs; buffalo horn decorations on the facade; no nails in traditional builds
Building Process & Rituals:
1. The tongkonan clan council (to parengnge') decides to build   a decision requiring consensus of all living descendants.
2. Ma'pakande deata: ritual feast offering to the deata (spirits) before ground is broken.
3. Main posts raised with chanting and the sacrifice of a buffalo   its blood is poured on the posts.
4. Roof built in layers over many weeks; each bamboo layer tied by hand.
5. Ma'bua' ceremony: the most sacred and expensive Toraja ceremony, held to inaugurate the tongkonan   involving mass buffalo sacrifice and days of feasting.
Philosophy & History (Fun Fact): Every tongkonan is both a house of the living and a house of the dead   it faces north (the direction of life) while the rice barn (alang) faces south (the direction of the dead). The number of buffalo horns stacked on the facade records every sacrifice ever made at that tongkonan   some have hundreds. The tongkonan is so sacred that Toraja emigrants around the world contribute money to maintain the family tongkonan back home, even if they never live in it.
Etiquette & Rules for Entering \/ Living: You must be invited by a clan member to approach a tongkonan. Never walk under the front overhang uninvited   it is considered part of the sacred threshold. Remove shoes. Sit only where directed by the host   seating encodes clan rank. During Rambu Solo' (funeral), follow all directions from the to parengnge'. Never photograph the interior without explicit permission. Pointing at the buffalo horns on the facade with a finger (rather than a thumb) is rude.
